_: The script as an artifact. Fill it, run script_check.mjs, and do not write
a line of composition code until it exits 0.
The five fields above `beats` are not paperwork — they are the five
questions the template has always told you to ASK THE USER rather than
guess. Guessing them is how both pilot demos were written, and both were
rejected by the first person who watched them.
audience: ONE named group, and what they do all day. 'Everyone' is not an audience.
category_noun: The word this audience would use for what kind of thing this is. Not your branding.
alternative: What they use instead today. If there is no alternative, there is no reason to switch.
mechanism: What the software DOES. One sentence, subject = the product.
claim: What the VIEWER GETS. One sentence, subject = the viewer. Ask 'so what?' of the mechanism until the answer happens to a person, then stop.
repeat_sentence: The one sentence a viewer says to a colleague afterwards. If you cannot write it, they will not say it.
assumed_known: Facts the audience already has before the video starts.
Keep this list SHORT and defend every entry — it is the escape hatch that
turns the cold-read ledger back into a rubber stamp.

jargon.term: every word on screen that is not everyday language
jargon.plain: what it means to someone who has never heard it
jargon.explained_in: the beat id where the video makes it mean something

beats.job: what this beat is FOR in the story — not what it contains
says: each line that appears, in order
beats.shows: what is on screen besides the words
needs: facts the viewer must already have
establishes: facts this beat hands the viewer
beats.names_category: true on the beat that says the category noun out loud, before 6s
beats.states_stakes: true on the beat that names what the viewer LOSES, in the first third
beats.shows_subject: true on any beat that shows the actual thing rather than describing it
beats.is_claim: true on exactly ONE beat — the one that lands the claim
